subject: physics_2
question_text: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. This is the book's SAQ 14: the printed Short Answer numbering runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and then jumps straight to 14, and that jump is the book's own — no questions 6 to 13 exist in this chapter. Cited "(June 2015 TS)"; the appearances field records the year 2015 and the board only, since it has no sitting field. PRINTED ERRORS CORRECTED: the book spells the question "neclear fussion" and heads the comparison columns "Fision" and "Fusion", and its row 6 states "Fision takes place at room temp." Fission is started by NEUTRON CAPTURE and needs no high temperature; it is FUSION that needs temperatures of the order of 10⁷ K, so the pair is written here as "fission needs no high temperature, fusion needs millions of kelvin". Hand-checked: about 200 MeV per fission of ²³⁵U, about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus formed from four hydrogen nuclei, and the energy per nucleon is larger for fusion (26.7/4 ≈ 6.7 MeV against 200/236 ≈ 0.85 MeV).

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: What each process is
steps.mark_note: Splitting a heavy nucleus against joining light nuclei
lines: Fission: a heavy nucleus such as U-235 splits
into two lighter nuclei when a moving neutron
strikes it, and energy is released.
Fusion: two light nuclei such as hydrogen join
to form a heavier nucleus, and energy is
released.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Splitting against joining, with one named nucleus on each side.
steps.why: Both release energy because both move the product closer to iron-56, where the binding energy per nucleon is largest: a heavy nucleus reaches it by splitting, a light one by joining.
common_mistakes: Saying fusion splits a nucleus. Fusion joins.
Leaving out the neutron that starts fission.

recall.must_convey: That fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into lighter nuclei, and fusion is the joining of light nuclei such as hydrogen into a heavier nucleus.
accept: heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei
light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus

steps.memory_tip: Fission: a heavy nucleus comes apart. Fusion: light nuclei come together.

steps.label: How each one starts
steps.mark_note: Neutron capture against very high temperature
lines: Fission is started when the nucleus captures a
neutron, so no high temperature is needed.
Fusion needs temperatures of the order of
10⁷ K and very high pressure, so that the
nuclei overcome their electric repulsion.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. This is the row students copy wrongly; state both conditions.
steps.why: The book prints "Fision takes place at room temp." That is loose: fission is not caused by temperature at all, it is caused by neutron capture, and the correct contrast is that fusion alone needs the enormous temperature.
common_mistakes: Writing that fission needs high temperature. It needs a neutron.
Writing that fusion happens at room temperature.

recall.must_convey: That fission is started by neutron capture and needs no high temperature, while fusion needs temperatures of the order of 10⁷ K and high pressure to overcome the electric repulsion.
accept: fission starts when a neutron is captured
fusion needs very high temperature and pressure
no high temperature is needed for fission

steps.memory_tip: Fission needs a bullet; fusion needs a furnace.

steps.label: Energy released
steps.mark_note: 200 MeV per fission; 26.7 MeV per fusion; more per nucleon in fusion
lines: Fission releases about 200 MeV each time one
heavy nucleus splits.
Fusion releases about 26.7 MeV for each helium
nucleus formed from four hydrogen nuclei.
Energy released per nucleon is less in fission
and more in fusion.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both numbers, and the per-nucleon comparison that reverses them.
steps.why: The totals and the per-nucleon values point opposite ways because fission shares 200 MeV among 236 nucleons while fusion shares 26.7 MeV among 4, so fusion gives about eight times as much per nucleon.
common_mistakes: Saying fusion releases more energy per reaction. Per reaction fission gives more; per nucleon fusion gives more.
Writing 200 eV or 26.7 eV. Both values are in MeV.

recall.must_convey: That fission releases about 200 MeV per nucleus split and fusion about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus formed, with more energy per nucleon in fusion.
accept: twenty six point seven MeV per fusion
energy per nucleon is more in fusion
reject: fission is started by a neutron

steps.memory_tip: 200 shared among 236, or 26.7 shared among 4 — that is why fusion wins per nucleon.

steps.label: Particles and applications
steps.mark_note: Neutrons and the atom bomb; protons, the hydrogen bomb and stars
lines: Fission involves neutrons, and the atom bomb
works on nuclear fission.
Fusion involves protons and other light nuclei,
and the hydrogen bomb and the stars work on
nuclear fusion.

lines.text: Fission splits heavy · Fusion joins light

steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. One application named for each process.
steps.why: The two bombs are the clearest marker of the difference: the atom bomb is an uncontrolled fission chain, the hydrogen bomb a fusion reaction that a fission bomb heats to ignition.
common_mistakes: Swapping the bombs. Atom bomb is fission, hydrogen bomb is fusion.
Saying stars run on fission. Stellar energy comes from fusion.

recall.must_convey: That fission involves neutrons and is the principle of the atom bomb, while fusion involves protons and light nuclei and is the principle of the hydrogen bomb and of stars.

steps.memory_tip: A for atom bomb, A for apart — fission. H for hydrogen bomb, H for hydrogen joining — fusion.

insider_note: Four marks, four points of difference, each written for BOTH processes. A list about fission alone earns half.
